group.title: Time and frequency
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Not often; only a few times.
examples: We {rarely} eat out because it costs a lot.
wrong: He rarely drinks coffee, so he has five cups every day.

words.meaning: At any time, used in questions and with not.
examples: Have you {ever} been to Japan?
wrong: "Have you ever been to Rome?" is a question only about next year.

examples: I go to the gym {once} a week, on Saturday.
wrong: She calls once a week: on Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

examples: I brush my teeth {twice} a day, morning and night.
wrong: He eats twice a day, so he has only one meal.

words.meaning: At the present time, compared with the past.
examples: {Nowadays} most people pay with their phones.
wrong: Nowadays people wrote letters by hand a hundred years ago.

words.meaning: Later, after something else has happened.
examples: We watched the film and went for pizza {afterwards}.
wrong: We had dinner afterwards, before the film started.

examples: The shop is open {daily} from nine to six.
wrong: The bus runs daily, but only on Sundays.

examples: The team meets {weekly} on Monday mornings.
wrong: We are paid weekly, once every two months.

examples: I pay the rent {monthly}, on the first day.
wrong: The magazine comes out monthly, every single morning.

examples: The festival takes place {yearly} in June.
wrong: The race happens yearly, about four times a week.

words.meaning: Often, and usually at the same times.
examples: She runs {regularly}, three times a week.
wrong: He goes to the dentist regularly; his last visit was twenty years ago.

examples: We {occasionally} go to the theater, maybe twice a year.
wrong: She occasionally drinks tea, about ten cups every day.

examples: Buses come {frequently}, every five minutes.
wrong: The train comes frequently, just once a day.

words.meaning: In the usual way; most of the time.
examples: I {normally} get up at seven, but today I slept late.
wrong: I normally go by bike, and today, as always, I took the bus for the first time.

examples: The baby is crying, so come here {at once}!
wrong: Please come at once; next week is fine.

words.meaning: At the beginning, before something changed.
examples: {At first} I didn’t like the city, but now I love it.
wrong: At first I loved it, and I still love it exactly the same.

examples: {At last} the rain stopped and we went outside.
wrong: The bus came at last, just one second after we arrived.

examples: We go to the beach {once in a while}, maybe three times a summer.
wrong: He calls his mom once in a while: every hour of every day.

examples: We got to the station {in time} to catch the train.
wrong: We got there in time, but the train had already left.

examples: I see my old school friends {from time to time}.
wrong: From time to time means at every single moment of the day.

examples: I eat chocolate {now and then}, maybe once a week.
wrong: He smokes now and then, forty cigarettes every day.

examples: My little brother asks questions {all the time}.
wrong: She talks all the time, so she almost never says a word.

examples: {These days} I work from home most of the week.
wrong: These days we didn’t have phones when I was a child.

words.meaning: After a long time or after many changes.
examples: We looked at ten flats, and {in the end} we chose the first one.
wrong: In the end, at the very start of the trip, we got lost.

examples: Let’s sit down and rest {for a while}.
wrong: He lived there for a while: his whole life, ninety years.

examples: I’ve read three chapters {so far}.
wrong: So far means at some time in the future.

examples: Sorry, she has {just} left the office.
wrong: He has just arrived; he got here last year.

examples: I moved here two years {ago}.
wrong: I will see you three days ago.

examples: Wash your hands and {then} sit down to eat.
wrong: First eat the cake and then bake it.

examples: I’m busy {at the moment}. Can I call you back?
wrong: He is sleeping at the moment, last Tuesday.

examples: I can’t talk {right now}; I’m driving.
wrong: She is eating right now, tomorrow at noon.

examples: Are you free {tonight}? Let’s see a film.
wrong: I went to the party tonight, three days ago.

examples: It {hardly ever} snows here, maybe once in ten years.
wrong: He hardly ever eats bread; he has it with every meal.

examples: I walk to work {most of the time}, but not when it rains.
wrong: Most of the time means just once or twice a year.

examples: I saw your brother at the store {the other day}.
wrong: I’ll meet him the other day, in two weeks.

examples: When the alarm rang, we left the building {right away}.
wrong: The fire alarm rang, so we left right away, two hours later.

words.meaning: At some time in the future, or on a day in the past.
examples: {One day} I want to visit Canada.
wrong: One day I’ll travel the world, but I never will.

words.meaning: Not until now, but probably later.
examples: Is dinner ready? {Not yet}, give me ten minutes.
wrong: Has the bus come? Not yet, it left an hour ago.

words.meaning: At some time in the future, even if you don’t know when.
examples: Don’t worry; he will call {sooner or later}.
wrong: Sooner or later means it will certainly never happen.

words.meaning: No longer; not now as in the past.
examples: I used to play the piano, but I don’t play {anymore}.
wrong: He doesn’t live here anymore, and he still lives here.
